paper_title: SemanTok: Predictable Semantic Tokens for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clip's global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply a representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, a target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, a flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: a 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model $3.4\times$ its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clips global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats VideoFlexTok AR model 3.4 its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens. Figure 1: From prompt with . . . orange basketball. . . (left, uCO3D), our SemanTok tokenizer lets 201M autoregressive (AR) model generate video that keeps the balls shape and appearance through the orbit with budget of only k=4 tokens per latent frame. VideoFlexTok: at the same models size the ball is semantically misaligned, and even an 11 larger AR model (2.29B) leaves its shape unstable up to k=64. So the smaller, faster model on SemanTok tokens matches or beats the larger one of VideoFlexTok. Right (Kinetics-600, class yoga): both tokenizers at the same 2.29B AR size, i.e., equal cost. SemanTok keeps complex body motion stable from k=16, and larger refines its appearance and motion. Meanwhile VideoFlexTok changes the scene between k=4 and k=16 and poorly simulates body motion. Both VideoFlexTok and SemanTok are variable-length: the AR model generates tokens coarse to fine, and any budget decodes to video. SemanTok prioritizes semantic content in its first tokens, so small already fixes what the clip contains. Pipeline in fig. 2; videos on the project page. 1 Figure 2: Overview. (1) Tokenizer training: encoder, FSQ, and diffusion decoder are trained jointly, with nested dropout so that the decoder can reconstruct the clip from any token prefix. SemanTok keeps this VideoFlexTok recipe (orange) and adds semantic supervision from frozen teacher: its features enter the encoder, and every retained prefix is trained to predict them (purple; details in fig. 3). (2) AR training and generation: with the tokenizer frozen, an AR model learns to predict its tokens in time-first, coarse-to-fine order, and the decoder trained in (1) renders any generated prefix as video.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video clips vary widely in complexity: static shot has few entities and little motion, while car chase has changing viewpoints and detail. To make such clips tractable, video models compress them into learned tokens that an autoregressive (AR) model predicts, as language model predicts text, and diffusion decoder renders into pixels (Yan et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2024a). These tokens must therefore be both easy to predict and informative enough to render. Yet standard video tokenizers map every clip to the same fixed-size spatiotemporal grid (NVIDIA, 2025; Tang et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024a). Because prediction cost grows with sequence length, simple and complex clips then get the same representational budget and the same compute. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers (Bachmann et al., 2025; Atanov et al., 2026) replace the fixed grid with linear sequence that can be meaningfully cropped to various lengths. At inference time, the application, not the model, selects budget and the autoregressive model predicts only up to that prefix length. Each prefix should support high-quality rendering, with additional tokens only increasing its specificity. We argue that this approach should aim to carry clips semantics in the coarse prefix, so that small AR model can settle on what the video should contain, before larger model spends capacity on fixing appearance details. Existing flexible tokenizers use representation alignment (REPA) (Yu et al., 2025) at an early decoder layer, showing that this improves downstream fidelity and semantic alignment (Atanov et al., 2026); this is mostly inspired by image tokenizers (Zhu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025). But that decoder also sees the noised latent, which at low noise meets the target almost regardless of the tokens  (fig. 9)  . For this, we propose SemanTok, flexible video tokenizer designed to prioritize semantic content early in an AR-model rollout (fig. 1; pipeline in fig. 2). We keep the original decoder REPA loss and the coarse-to-fine recipe. Frozen DINOv2 features (Oquab et al., 2024) enter the encoder alongside the video latents. Auxiliary heads then read only the retained token prefix and reconstruct the DINO features. We call these two uses of the teacher semantic supervision. No loss assigns information to particular tokens; nested dropout concentrates the most relevant information in the earliest ones. The result is variable-length semantic code: every prefix, at any budget, carries the teachers view of the clip. The same prefix that these pathways make more semantic is also easier for an AR model to predict. At the same length, the AR model then needs fewer bits to code it: SemanTok keeps what the clip contains early and defers part of the pixel detail the AR model could not predict, prefix-level form of the compressiongeneration trade-off (Ramanujan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). We evaluate SemanTok (section 3) on fidelity and semantic alignment in the generation and groundtruth-token reconstruction settings for video (section 4). We score seven AR sizes (49M2.29B) across token budgets, on class-conditioned (Kinetics-600) and text-conditioned (uCO3D). Seven findings emerge (section 5): 1 SemanTok exhibits high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size. 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats VideoFlexTok AR model 3.4 its size (figs. 1, 4, 5 and 13; see exception 7 ). 2 2 Increasing SemanTok model size further improves fidelity. The smaller SemanTok AR model exceeds the larger VideoFlexTok AR model in Kinetics-600 class accuracy (semantic alignment). Increasing model size further improves fidelity (gFVD) (figs. 5 to 7 and 16). 3 SemanTok is able to maintain semantic alignment over out-of-distribution classes. Both tokenizer reconstruction and AR generation show the generalization capability of SemanTok on held-out classes (table 1 and figs. 8 and 17; see exception 7 ). 4 SemanTok achieves higher decoder-REPA semantic alignment at all noise levels, including the pure noise setting. (figs. 9 and 18; see exception 7 ). 5 SemanTok has high fidelity on reconstruction as well as generation. VideoFlexTok performs worse on generation than reconstruction, while SemanTok performs well on both (figs. 10, 12 and 14 and table 2; see exception 7 ). 6 SemanToks has better generation fidelity from its earlier tokens, which are cheaper to predict. Under the same AR model, generation at k=16 costs about 32% fewer bits per token, and pixel detail is deferred to later tokens, not discarded (figs. 11 and 20). 7 SemanTok with 1 token per frame struggles to serve every objective. At k=1, SemanTok trails VideoFlexTok in semantic alignment with mostly clean latent. Surprisingly, SemanTok still keeps its class-accuracy lead at every budget (fig. 4 and tables 6 to 10).

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Token-based video generation. Video models predict discrete tokens from grid tokenizers, autoregressively (Yan et al., 2021; Kondratyuk et al., 2024) or by masked prediction (Villegas et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024a), and world models use the same recipe for action-conditioned rollouts (Bruce et al., 2024; NVIDIA, 2025) or predict self-supervised features instead of pixels (Assran et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025). In hybrids, AR fixes the content and diffusion renders it (Li et al., 2024; 2025b); VAR instead orders prediction coarse-to-fine across scales (Tian et al., 2024). Every grid location still reaches the generator. Ordered and flexible tokenizers. TiTok and LARP compress images and videos into 1D token sequences (Yu et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025). Nested dropout and Matryoshka losses order such codes by importance (Rippel et al., 2014; Kusupati et al., 2022): ElasticTok drops token suffixes (Yan et al., 2025), Semanticist finds PCA-like, semantics-first ordering (Wen et al., 2025), and FlexTok and VideoFlexTok make every prefix decodable, with REPA on an early decoder layer (Bachmann et al., 2025; Atanov et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025). ReToK strengthens decoder alignment for shorter prefixes (Fu et al., 2026), LoST aligns ordered 3D latents with DINO (Dutt et al., 2026), and SpeechTokenizer distills teacher into its first audio level (Zhang et al., 2024). SemanTok trains every retained prefix of flexible video code to predict the teacher without the noised latent, which no prior video tokenizer does to our knowledge. Tokenizers for generation, not reconstruction. Reconstruction alone does not make latent easy to model. DiGIT, MAETok, VA-VAE, ImageFolder, GigaTok, and UniTok align or predict foundation-model features to improve generation (Zhu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Xiong et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025); REPA-E trains the VAE through the REPA loss (Leng et al., 2025), and RAE diffuses directly in frozen DINO features (Zheng et al., 2026). LARP and CRT shape the code with an AR prior, trading reconstruction for generation (Wang et al., 2025; Ramanujan et al., 2025), consistent with the perceptiondistortion trade-off (Blau & Michaeli, 2018). These works use fixed-length, mostly image, codes. We place semantics in the early prefixes of flexible video tokenizer, where small AR model spends its budget.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: We compare SemanTok to its closest prior work VideoFlexTok which differs only in semantic supervision, at the same codebook, sequence length, and AR recipe. We ask how that supervision changes generation. First, we measure how fidelity and semantic alignment change with AR model size 1 , how larger and longer-trained AR models improve fidelity further 2 , and whether semantic alignment holds on out-of-distribution classes 3 . We then examine how the token prefix affects decoder-REPA semantic alignment 4 . We measure the difference between generation fidelity and reconstruction fidelity i.e. realization gap 5 , and trace SemanToks generation gain to specific tokens 6 . Finally, we report where SemanTok falls behind: at one token per frame 7 . Data We use Kinetics-600 for class-to-video setting with controlled action label, and uCO3D for text-to-video over objects including an in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) (never seen in training) class split. Model Following VideoFlexTok (Atanov et al., 2026), SemanTok shares the backbone, decoder REPA, codebook, sequence length, sampling settings, LLaMA-style AR recipe, and pixel resolution (17 frames at 128 128 on both datasets). SemanTok changes the encoder input and adds the tokenlevel objectives of section 3 using DINOv2. Evaluation The metrics we evaluate SemanTok on are: Fidelity i.e. closeness in appearance to real video, measured by gFVD and gFID. Semantic alignment i.e. whether the video shows the conditioned content: class accuracy, text video cosine similarity (ViCLIP), videovideo cosine similarity in ViCLIP space (ClipV). For the tokenizer we also report decoder semantic alignment (REPA), the DINOv2 cosine similarity of the decoder-REPA readout. On Kinetics-600, class accuracy is closed-set UMT-L top-1 (Li et al., 2023) over 2,048 generated clips. On uCO3D, it is nearest-class-mean top-1 in InceptionV3 space over 2,560 clips per split, 5 Figure 4: 1 SemanTok improves generation at every compute budget on Kinetics-600 and uCO3D. Generation versus AR inference FLOPs per clip. Each faded curve is one AR size (colour) sweeping the token budget from 1 to 256 tokens per frame. Black: the best score each tokenizer reaches at given compute. SemanToks envelope is better over most of the compute range. Figure 5: 2 Fidelity scales with AR model size for both VideoFlexTok and SemanTok, while the semantic-alignment gap between does not close. Figure 6: 2 Semantic alignment gap between SemanTok and VideoFlexTok closes slower than the fidelity gap between them. which stays defined for held-out classes. Additional details, including bootstrap intervals, the scope of our ablations, and the tokenizer training budget, are in section D. Scalability and efficiency. We sweep seven AR sizes from 49M to 2.29B parameters, their inference FLOPs, and 1.33B AR model trained from 1.3B to 65.5B tokens. We measure efficiency at two levels. At the model level, it is the AR size needed to reach given fidelity and semantic alignment. At the token level, it is how hard the tokens are to predict: the validation cross-entropy (in bits per token). All AR models train on all 256 tokens per latent frame, and the budget 1, 2, 4, . . . , 256 is chosen only at evaluation. { }

sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: 1 SemanTok exhibits high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size. With each tokenizer at its best k, every SemanTok AR model reaches lower gFVD and gFID and higher class accuracy than the VideoFlexTok AR model of the same size, on both Kinetics-600 and uCO3D (figs. 4 and 5). On Kinetics-600, SemanTok lowers gFVD by 1124% and gFID by 517% and raises class accuracy by 2561%, with the largest gains for the smallest AR models. On uCO3D, SemanTok improves gFVD, gFID, and class accuracy by 213%, 58%, and 2230%, with no clear trend in AR model size. At the single budget k=16, an 85M SemanTok 6 Figure 7: 2 SemanTok stays ahead at both AR model sizes.Class-to-video rollouts for one Kinetics600 playing-guitar label. At 201M, SemanTok degrades slowly over time, while VideoFlexTok is sharp only at t=1. Videos on the project page. AR model beats VideoFlexTok AR model of every size and budget, up to 2.29B, in gFID on both datasets and in gFVD on Kinetics-600. The 85M SemanTok AR model matches that VideoFlexTok AR model in uCO3D gFVD and beats it in class accuracy on both datasets. In semantic alignment even the smallest SemanTok model (49M) beats the best VideoFlexTok AR model of any size, up to 2.29B, in class accuracy, ClipV, and ViCLIP on both datasets. On Kinetics600, SemanToks class accuracy is 0.631 against 0.560 for the 2.29B VideoFlexTok model. More tokens cost more AR compute and their generations degrade in gFVD beyond certain point. However, VideoFlexTok gives worse gFVD after only k=16, while SemanTok does not degrade until after k=32. 2 Increasing SemanTok model size further improves fidelity. Larger or longer-trained AR models mostly trim the compounding error of the token rollout, which improves fidelity. The same scaling gains less in semantic alignment, because what the clip shows is largely decided by the first tokens, which come from the tokenizer ( 6 ). Figure 5 separates the two axes by AR size. SemanToks best-k class accuracy and ClipV lie above VideoFlexTok at every size. Fidelity improves with AR model size for both tokenizers, and SemanTok reaches given fidelity with fewer parameters. From 49M to 2.29B, SemanToks best-k gFVD falls from 224 to 202 on Kinetics-600 and from 218 to 197 on uCO3D. SemanToks benefit is largest where AR capacity is scarce: at k=64, SemanToks gFID gain over VideoFlexTok halves from 49M to 2.29B. Training budget behaves like model size  (fig. 6)  . For the 1.33B AR model on Kinetics-600, SemanToks best-k gFVD lead shrinks from 28% to 9% by 26B tokens, then holds at 1114%. SemanToks class-accuracy lead on Kinetics-600 persists, at 30% after 65.5B tokens. So 5 more training buys VideoFlexTok some fidelity, but not semantic alignment. On uCO3D, SemanToks ClipV nearly saturates by 13B tokens and stays above VideoFlexToks. As one rollout demonstrates  (fig. 7)  , scaling to 2.29B sharpens the videos of both tokenizers, but SemanToks maintains the lead. 3 SemanTok is able to maintain semantic alignment over out-of-distribution classes. We test this on uCO3D, whose out-of-distribution (OOD) object classes are never seen in training, unlike its in-distribution (ID) classes. SemanTok leads on semantic-alignment in both tokenizer reconstruction and AR generation. SemanTok prefixes recover the object class at lower better than VideoFlexToks on both ID and OOD clips  (fig. 8)  . At k=16 on uCO3D, SemanToks reconstructions score higher ClipV and class accuracy than VideoFlexToks but about 2.7 dB lower PSNR  (table 2)  . The lead carries over to AR generation: with 201M AR model at k=16, SemanTok raises generated class accuracy over VideoFlexTok by 24% on ID clips and by 29% on OOD classes, and improves ClipV on both  (table 1)  . ViCLIP favors SemanTok from k=16 on, but not at k=4. 4 SemanTok achieves higher decoder-REPA semantic alignment at all noise levels, including the pure noise setting. Decoder REPA aligns an early decoder layer with DINOv2 features(section 3). The decoder also sees partly noised latent, which can supply part of this target without the tokens. We therefore read out the REPA projection on both datasets while varying the noise level σ of the decoder input  (fig. 9)  . For generation from pure noise, SemanToks readout has higher DINOv2 cosine similarity than VideoFlexToks at every k. At k=32 on uCO3D, SemanToks pure-noise readout reaches the similarity that VideoFlexTok reaches only with 75%- clean latent (0.721 vs. 0.716). At k=256 the latent adds almost nothing to SemanToks readout, but over 11 more to VideoFlexToks (section C). (The exception is the smallest budgets with mostly clean latent, see 7 ). Figure 8: 3 SemanTok reconstructions on uCO3D from ground-truth tokens recover the original object class at an earlier than VideoFlexTok; for both in-distribution (ID) clips and out-of-distribution (OOD) clips. Figure 9: 4 SemanToks decoder-REPA readout depends less on the noised latent and achieves higher REPAalignment than VideoFlexToks. 5 SemanTok has high fidelity on reconstruction as well as generation (see fig. 10). VideoFlexTok reconstructs somewhat better in PSNR and rFVD, but it loses more fidelity in generation, so its realization gap is wider. SemanTok has the lower gFVD at every AR size, at both k=64 and k=128, and hence lower realization gap. (On Kinetics-600, generated class accuracy can exceed reconstruction because the AR model sees the class label.) 6 SemanToks generation fidelity gain comes from its earlier tokens, which are cheaper to predict. Two measurements on Kinetics-600 show that SemanToks gain is concentrated in the earlier tokens. First, we force the first ground-truth tokens per frame and free-run to k=256 (fig. 11(a)). With nothing forced, SemanToks gFVD is 23% lower than VideoFlexToks at 201M. SemanToks lead vanishes once the first 1664 tokens are forced, after which VideoFlexToks better-reconstructing tail edges ahead. Second, SemanToks prefix is cheaper to predict (fig. 11(b)). The bits the AR model needs per predicted token is measured by cross-entropy. At k=16, SemanTok needs 32% fewer bits per token than VideoFlexTok (8.8 vs. 12.9 at 201M). SemanToks marginal entropy is only about one bit lower, so most of the saving comes from context. It is to be noted that the cost saving does not come from repetition: SemanTok repeats tokens less often overall than VideoFlexTok (section D.4). SemanToks cheap prefix keeps the semantics and defers pixel detail. SemanToks first 4 tokens cost 37 bits per frame, yet nearly match the class accuracy of VideoFlexToks first 32 tokens (405 bits, table 2). Later tokens restore part of that detail, and the generative decoder fills in the rest. 7 SemanTok with one token per frame struggles to serve every objective. This fact is consistent throughout our experiments (tables 6 to 10). SemanToks losses to VideoFlexTok that clear the bootstrap intervals are all on uCO3D at 4, mostly gFID and ClipV at k=1. On Kinetics-600, SemanTok is never significantly worse. Limitation : Because SemanTok prioritizes semantic alignment over reconstruction, it struggles to reconstruct the same colors/appearance details at lower token budgets.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce SemanTok, an AR video generation tokenizer and prediction module, which emphasizes semantic alignment at flexible token budget. Semantic supervision from frozen teacher, as encoder input and as target for every retained prefix, makes token prefixes richer in semantics ( 1 ), lends to scaling in size ( 2 ), maintains generalization in out-of-distribution setting ( 3 ), has better semantic alignment in high noise inputs ( 4 ), performs well at both reconstruction and generation ( 5 ), and is cheaper to predict ( 6 ). Future directions include optimizing predictability directly, organizing early prefixes with videonative or language-aligned teachers, and using such prefixes as compact states for action-conditioned world models.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Both tokenizers share the architecture and objective in section 3. SemanToks changes are the DINO encoder input, the class-token injection, and the two prediction heads with their loss weights. Table 3 lists tokenizer settings and training budgets. Tables 4 and 5 list the AR size ladder, learning rates, and dataset-specific regularization. Section gives the sampling settings, including the budgetdependent AR guidance. It also describes each metric and its readout model: FVD, FID, ViCLIP, ClipV, UMT-L, and the nearest-class-mean protocol for held-out classes. All datasets and pretrained models are public and cited where they are first used.

Only the reference differs, as each metric requires: rFVD against the reference distribution, ViCLIP against the caption, and PSNR/SSIM per clip against VAEGT. sections.title: C WHERE THE TOKENIZERS KEEP DINO SEMANTICS
sections.content: Both tokenizers train an early decoder layer to predict DINOv2 patch features through decoder REPA. We read that projection out without any training, which asks where the decoder finds its semantics. We keep the first tokens per frame and fix the decoder noise level σ, with the same noise seed for both tokenizers and every k. At σ=1 the decoder input is pure noise, so any DINO content in the readout comes from the token prefix. Generation starts from this state, with ARsampled tokens as the only input. sections.title: D EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: D.1 TOKENIZER TRAINING VideoFlexTok and SemanTok share the tokenizer architecture and optimizer in table 3. Both use frozen VidTok-128 VAE, an 18-layer encoder, an 18-layer time-causal decoder, and sixdimensional FSQ bottleneck. Nested dropout samples uniformly from powers of two through k=256. The decoder REPA weight is 1.0 in both arms. SemanTok additionally concatenates frozen DINOv2-L features to the encoder input with learned Its dense and class-token prediction losses each have weight 0.5. The DINO linear projection. features are 16 1024 per latent frame, and the class token is projected into register token 16 zero with zero-initialized layer. These heads are causal over latent frames. The paper results use tokenizers trained on 66B tokens on uCO3D and 131B tokens on Kinetics-600. Ablations. Early in the project, we ran smaller-scale ablations to narrow down the design. They compared SigLIP 2 (Tschannen et al., 2025) with DINOv2 as the semantic teacher, and we kept DINOv2. They also favoured using both forms of semantic supervision together: frozen DINOv2 features at the encoder input, as dense patch features and as class-token bias on the first register token, and explicit DINO targets on every retained token prefix. D.2 TOKENIZER TRAINING BUDGET The released VideoFlexTok tokenizer uses roughly 400B training tokens on Kinetics-600. We train both arms for 131B tokens on Kinetics-600 and 66B on uCO3D, less than third of that budget, and our Kinetics-600 tokenizers were still improving. AR models trained on earlier tokenizer checkpoints show SemanToks lead at every checkpoint, with no sign of the gap closing  (fig. 19)  , so longer budget is unlikely to reverse it. Kinetics-600 still improves. From 66B to 131B tokens, both tokenizers reconstruct better at k=256. These numbers score 2,560 clips against their VAE-decoded ground truth, not table 2s 2,048-clip real reference bank, so absolute values and the k=256 rFVD ordering differ from that table. VideoFlexToks rFVD falls from 78.4 to 59.2, PSNR rises from 19.0 to 19.7 dB, and class accuracy from 0.418 to 0.491. SemanToks rFVD falls from 71.0 to 54.9, PSNR rises from 18.1 to 18.5 dB, and class accuracy from 0.466 to 0.516. We therefore use the 131B checkpoints, and longer budget would likely improve both arms further. uCO3D overfits after 66B. We also continued both uCO3D tokenizers to 98B tokens. Reconstruction at k=16 got worse for both (256 clips, k=16): PSNR fell from 18.66 to 18.07 dB for VideoFlexTok and from 15.96 to 15.56 dB for SemanTok, and rFVD rose from 351 to 373 and from 425 to 469. For 49M AR model at k=16, SemanToks class accuracy and ClipV also dipped 205). We slightly (0.309 attribute the decline to overfitting on the small uCO3D training set and report the 66B checkpoints for both arms. 0.725), although its gFVD improved (226 0.302 and 0.731 The uCO3D lead holds throughout training. To test whether SemanTok only converges faster, we took six tokenizer checkpoints between 6.6B and 66B training tokens and trained fresh 49M AR model on each ones tokens for 8k steps  (fig. 19)  . This recipe is cheaper than section 5s (unaugmented tokens, fewer AR steps), so compare only within the figure. SemanTok has higher ClipV at every checkpoint and both k. At 66B tokens it scores 0.710 vs. 0.680 at k=16 and 0.669 vs. 0.627 at k=256. Its gFVD is lower at every checkpoint at k=256 and from 26B tokens at k=16, reaching 198 vs. 224 and 386 vs. 452 at 66B. ViCLIP and class accuracy show the same ordering (class accuracy 0.295 vs. 0.214 at k=16, 66B). VideoFlexTok gains little after 26B tokens and closes none of these gaps. At k=256 SemanToks own gFVD rises after 26B, so its lead there narrows from 199 to 66. The Kinetics-600 lead holds throughout training. We repeat this test on Kinetics-600 with the full recipe of section 5 rather than cheap probe: for tokenizer checkpoints at 26B, 66B, 98B, and 131B training tokens we train 201M AR model for 20k steps on each ones tokens and score it with the protocol of fig. 4 (fig. 19, bottom row). SemanTok has higher class accuracy and ClipV at every 19 checkpoint and every k, and lower gFVD at every checkpoint from k=8. The gaps do not close with training: at k=16, gFVD is 291 vs. 349 at 26B and 217 vs. 273 at 131B, and class accuracy is 0.413 vs. 0.205 and 0.639 vs. 0.422. At 66B tokens, half the budget, SemanTok already beats VideoFlexTok at 131B on all three metrics at every 4, so its lead is not an artifact of the 131B budget. Figure 19: SemanToks lead holds throughout tokenizer training on both datasets. Each point is an AR model trained on one tokenizer checkpoints tokens. Top: uCO3D, 49M AR probe trained for 8k steps, official validation split. Bottom: Kinetics-600, 201M AR model with the recipe and evaluation of fig. 4. No gap closes as the tokenizer trains longer. Released checkpoint. We cannot compare against the released VideoFlexTok Kinetics-600 checkpoint. Its decoder is fine-tuned for bidirectional attention, whereas the paper describes such finetuning only for Panda-70M (Chen et al., 2024). The reconstruction metrics we measured for this checkpoint do not match those reported in the paper, likely because of this deviation. No timecausal checkpoint is released, so we retrain VideoFlexTok with the same time-causal recipe, data, and budget as SemanTok. D.3 AUTOREGRESSIVE TRAINING The downstream AR model is LLaMA-style causal decoder with RMSNorm and SwiGLU. At depth d, its width is 64d and it has attention heads. It trains on the time-first sequence of K=1,280 scalar indices τt,i with global batch 512. budget corresponds to the first scalar indices, or token positions per latent frame. All runs use AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.05, gradient clipping 1.0, bf16, 2.5% warmup, and cosine decay to one percent of peak LR. Head bias uses the log-unigram initialization. Depth-scaled initialization is disabled. We otherwise follow VideoFlexTok. For uCO3D only, we increase trunk dropout and conditioning dropout after observing overfitting. D.4 EVALUATION PROTOCOLS AR generation. We follow the VideoFlexTok evaluation pipeline. Sampling uses temperature 1.0 without top-k or top-p truncation. The decoder uses 50 flow steps and guidance 3.0. Kinetics-600 AR guidance is 3.0 for , and 1.0 thereafter, following the budget dependence reported by VideoFlexTok. uCO3D uses AR guidance 3.0 at every budget.
